newsitem.title: PERU: Red Cross ends hostage role amid Peru controversy.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross ends hostage role amid Peru controversy.

text.p: The Red Cross said on Friday it has finished its work in Peru's hostage saga, but could find itself embroiled in controversy after the bloody rescue of 71 VIPs held by Tupac Amaru rebels at the Japanese ambassador's home.
"There is no role for us. We were asked to help during the crisis. Right now there is no real place for us," Red Cross spokeswoman Cecile Baux told Reuters.

The organisation hopes to return to its normal work in Peru, including resuming visits to jailed Tupac Amaru rebels that the government stopped soon after 14 heavily armed members of the group stormed the mansion on Dec. 17, Baux said.

But the Red Cross, which repeatedly ruffled government feathers during the siege, could find itself dragged back into the hostage saga as reports emerged that Peru's military prepared hostages for the strike with a device smuggled inside.

"Everything we took into the residence was checked by both sides. The police and the MRTA both had the opportunity to check everything," Baux said of the Red Cross daily shuttle service which ferried supplies to hostages inside.
Asked if she believed the organisation had been duped into passing devices to captives, Baux said: "Everything the Red Cross did was done with transparency."
Peace talks guarantors and independent doctors accompanying Red Cross officials also made regular visits into the mined and booby-trapped compound during the 126-day siege.
Security forces sources claimed they monitored the rebels' activity with listening gadgets slipped inside books, cups and chess sets given to hostages by the Red Cross.

The militray, which caught the rebels off guard playing soccer in a reception room, ordered its strike after communicating with a captive police chief on one device smuggled into the mansion inside a book, they added.

Unwitting help from the Red Cross could be acutely embarrassing for the humanitarian organisation, as Tuesday's raid provoked a rash of allegations that troops executed at least two rebels and killed one other who tried to surrender.
One hostage, two commandos and all 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels died in the raid launched from a warren of tunnels dug under the residence.
The Red Cross' chief official in Peru, Michel Minnig, has said his officials knew nothing of a pending raid or material smuggled inside the residence.
Minnig became a protagonist in a standoff that grabbed headlines around the world as he worked tirelessly -- and in the end fruitlessly -- as a peace broker between the government and rebels.

But while the Swiss aid worker became a reluctant celebrity, eulogised by local media, his assistant, Juan Pedro Schaerer, angered the Peruvian government sufficeiently to be asked to leave the country.
Government officials told Minnig on Wednesday that the Peruvian authorities had "lost confidence" in Schaerer, Baux said.
"In the absence of more specific details, the Red Cross considers that its delegate did not overstep the mandate entrusted to him," she added.
